claims.text: HfZrTiTa0.53 should be processed by approximately 50% cold rolling followed by annealing at about 750 °C for 30 seconds.
Cold rolling followed by rapid annealing will refine the grain structure.
The proposed treatment will produce a more uniform grain structure.
The proposed treatment will balance or adjust dislocation density.
Cold rolling introduces a high dislocation density.
Rapid annealing at the proposed conditions will refine grains without full recrystallization.
The modified microstructure will facilitate activation of additional slip systems.
Grain-boundary-mediated plasticity and more homogeneous deformation will increase tensile ductility and uniform elongation.
The treatment will improve elongation by roughly 20–30% relative to the reported 13.5% strain.
Uniform tensile elongation will increase from 13.5% to approximately 17–18%.
Yield strength will remain within approximately 5% of the 786 MPa baseline.
The treatment will preserve comparable impact-triggered chemical-energy release.
Untreated HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
Untreated HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
Untreated HfZrTiTa0.53 has a terminal strain of 13.5%.
The predicted improvement applies at room temperature and strain rates near 1×10^-3 s^-1.
Outcomes at substantially different temperatures or strain rates are uncertain.
Excessive processing may compromise strength or energy-release characteristics.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% value is introduced as terminal strain, but the prediction treats it as the baseline uniform tensile elongation. Terminal strain and uniform tensile elongation are not interchangeable metrics.
A rise from 13.5% to 18% is about a 33% relative increase, exceeding the stated 20–30% improvement range.
The prediction concerns uniform tensile elongation of 17–18%, whereas the falsification threshold is stated as approximately 16.2% total elongation, changing both the metric and the target.
The conditions characterize processing and testing as quasi-static, while the experiment also calls for impact penetration tests, which are dynamic rather than quasi-static.
